Stage 3 · Grammar

How long? — for and since

Saying how long something has been true, and when it started.

Read these four sentences from the lesson.
  • I’ve been a newspaper journalist since 2001.
  • I’ve worked here for five years.
  • Ana has worked in the same laboratory since 2011.
  • How long have you had your phone?
Look at the words after for and after since. What is the difference?
The choice
for + how long it has lastedsince + when it started
five yearsI’ve worked here for five years.2011She’s worked here since 2011.
two monthsHe’s been a nurse for two months.MarchHe’s been a nurse since March.
a long timeWe’ve known them for a long time.I left schoolWe’ve known them since I left school.
agesI haven’t seen her for ages.last FridayI haven’t seen her since last Friday.
The form
 PositiveNegativeQuestionShort answer
I / you / we / theyI ’ve worked here for five years.I haven’t worked here for long.Have you worked here for long?Yes, I have. / No, I haven’t.
he / she / itShe ’s worked there since 2011.He hasn’t worked there since May.Has she worked there since 2011?Yes, she has. / No, she hasn’t.
How long…?How long have you been a nurse?  ·  How long has he known her?  —  the answer is always for… or since…
Still true nowI’ve worked here for five years. ✓ I work here now.
I worked here for five years. ✗ I don’t work here any more.
have / has for / since

FORM. have / has + past participle. I’ve worked · she’s worked · they’ve been.

USE. It started in the past and it is still true now. That is why the present simple and the past simple both fail here.

THE CHOICE. for + a length of time · since + the point it started.

Not “I work here since 2019”, not “I am working here for five years”, not “since five years”.

This is the last stop for the Present Perfect thread that started in Unit 6.

FORM. have / has + past participle: I’ve worked · she’s worked · we’ve known · he’s been. In speech the have almost disappears: I’ve sounds like ive, she’s like shiz. That is why it is easy to miss when you listen.

USE. The action or situation started in the past and it is still true at this moment. I’ve worked here for five years means I am still here today. If you say I worked here for five years, you have left.

THE CHOICE. for answers how long? — for two months, for eight years, for ages, for a long time. since answers starting when? — since March, since 2011, since Monday, since I left school. If the words after it name a period, use for. If they name a moment on the calendar, use since.

Three mistakes to watch: “I work here since 2019” (present simple instead of present perfect) · “I am working here for five years” (present continuous) · “since five years” (five years is a length, so it needs for).

One more thing worth filing away. How long have you been here? asks about now. How long were you there? asks about a job or a place you have already left — and that one takes the past simple.

Real questions from the coursebook recording.

Listen. In fast speech have and has lose their vowel. Which one do you hear?

Two recordings, one question each. You are only listening for have or has.

AHow long ____ you worked here?
BHow long ____ he known her?

The full word is almost never said. Listen for the person before it — you takes have, he takes has.

Full grammar reference — Present Perfect with for and since

Form

PositiveI have worked here for six years. · She’s been a judge since 2015.
NegativeI haven’t seen him for ages.
QuestionHow long have you worked here?
Short answersYes, I have. / No, she hasn’t.
The pairfor + a period · since + a point in time

When and why we use it

  • This structure describes something that started in the past and is still true now.
  • For answers ‘how long?’: for six years, for two days, for ages.
  • Since answers ‘from when?’: since 2015, since Monday, since I left school.
  • Since can be followed by a clause in the Past Simple: I’ve known her since we were at school.

Signal words

how long · for · since · all my life · ever since

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I work here since 2019. → I have worked here since 2019.Started in the past, still true.
  • I’ve been here since six years. → … for six years.A period takes for.
  • I’ve lived here for 2019. → … since 2019.A point takes since.
  • How long do you work here? → How long have you worked here?The question needs the Present Perfect.

Don’t confuse it with

I’ve worked here for six years (still here) against I worked there for six years (finished; I have left).

Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

How long people really stay in the job they have.

Before you read: in the UK, how long does the average worker stay with one employer?

Choose one, then read and find out if you were right.

There is no right answer to guess. Guessing just makes you look for the number.

The people who stay, and the people who move

Fifty years ago, most people chose one profession and stayed in it. Their parents had done the same. A man who started work on a building site at eighteen often left the same company at sixty-five. People used to talk about “a job for life”, and they meant it.

Today the picture is different. In the United Kingdom the average worker stays with one employer for about five years. Some professions hold on to their staff for much longer. Judges have worked in the same court for twenty or thirty years. Nurses stay in health care even when they move hospital: one survey found that a nurse has usually worked in the profession for eleven years before she thinks about leaving it. In construction and in sales the numbers are much lower, and many people move on after two or three years.

Money is not the whole answer. Ana Ruiz has worked in the same laboratory since 2011. “I could earn more somewhere else,” she says, “but I have known these people for fourteen years.” Tom Baker, an accountant, moved four times in six years. “I used to think that was normal,” he says. “Now I have been with this business for eight years and I don’t want to move again. The clients know me. The office is open-plan and noisy, but the staff are good. That matters more than I thought it would.”

There is one more thing the numbers do not show. People who stay a long time are often the ones who changed something inside the job — a new team, a new zone of the building, a different day-to-day routine — instead of changing the job itself.

Sources. Written for this course from public labour-market data: UK Office for National Statistics, job tenure series · NHS Digital, workforce statistics · OECD, Employment by job tenure intervals. Figures are rounded. Ana Ruiz and Tom Baker are composites written for this course; no words are attributed to a real person.
